tables.how: The latest version of each return of the organizations the City funds, Schedule I Part II. A grant is listed when the recipient’s stated section is 501(c)(4), or its name reads as a political body (action fund, political issues committee, political action committee, ballot measure), and the grants to that recipient come to $5,000 or more. The case adds up the four largest whose section is 501(c)(4) or whose name says political committee: $320,000. The other rows are listed so that everything the rule caught can be seen: several are grants by a fiscal sponsor to a project’s own action fund, and some recipients are stated on the return as charities. One relationship the rule caught is left out because the recipient is a concrete company whose name contains the letters “Pac”.
tables.limits: A charity may fund lobbying and issue advocacy from unrestricted private donations, and many keep an affiliated advocacy organization for exactly that. The return does not say which money the grant came from, and nothing here shows that City money or other restricted money was used, or that the recipient spent the grant on San Francisco candidates or measures. A name with “action fund” in it is not proof of political work, and the section is whatever the charity typed.

tables.limits: City payments are for services under contracts and grants. Setting them beside a grant to a political arm shows only that the same organization did both; money is fungible and only the organization’s own books can show which dollars went where.
